proof_summary: After clearing the factorial denominator, the proof uses LTE and the multiplicative order of 2 modulo an odd prime divisor \(p\mid n\) to show that the product \(\prod_{k<n-1}(2^k-1)\) has strictly larger \(p\)-adic valuation than \((n-1)!\), so the resulting sum lacks the extra factor of \(p\) required by \(n!\); powers of two are excluded similarly by a one-unit mismatch in the 2-adic valuation. Once \(n\) is prime, if the order of 2 were less than \(n-1\), its corresponding factor would make the product vanish modulo \(n\), and the product identity together with Wilson’s theorem would force both \(a(n-1)\) and then \(2^{n-2}\) to vanish modulo \(n\), a contradiction.
